newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Human rights differences cloud ASEAN-EU future.
newsitem.headline: Human rights differences cloud ASEAN-EU future.

text.p: Southeast Asian and European Union foreign ministers questioned on Friday whether their economic ties could survive fundamental differences over human rights, but eventually agreed on ways to build trade.
The 22 foreign ministers from the European Union (EU) and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) issued a Final Declaration that outlined modest steps to increase business and trade ties.

But frank discussions over Burma, East Timor and human rights in general led ministers to question whether meetings between the two regional blocs should continue, Singaporean Foreign Minister and conference co-chairman Shanmugam Jayakumar told a news conference.
He said they decided they should. "The overwhelming consensus that emerged was that, yes, there are these challenges, but relations will flourish notwithstanding the challenges."
The ASEAN-EU meeting is to be followed on Saturday by a separate Asia-Europe meeting (ASEM).
ASEAN -- Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam -- would be joined by Japan, China and South Korea on the Asian side.
The 15 members of the European Union make up the European side -- but not under the EU umbrella.
Some ASEAN senior officials have begun to question whether the meetings with the EU should be scrapped in favour of the ASEM process.
"You have to ask yourself: What is the future of ASEAN-EU? Should it be replaced by ASEM? I don't know. I'll have to sleep on it," one senior official said.
Dutch Foreign Minister Hans Van Mierlo, the current EU president and conference co-chairman, argued that bloc-to-bloc talks between ASEAN and the EU were vital.

"The question is whether our blocs are real or not," he told the news conference. "So if the blocs are real, you should not run away from that reality... I'm absolutely convinced we should go on this road."
Both sides acknowledge the potential for cooperation is immense.

The EU single market is the world's largest trading entity. ASEAN is evolving a free trade area by 2003 that would contain more than 500 million consumers with a combined gross domestic product of a half-trillion dollars.

But ASEAN officials have long expressed frustration that the EU "can be held hostage" to the foreign policy of one its members -- Portugal's insistence, for example, on raising the East Timor issue at these meetings.
ASEAN officials are also unhappy that the European Parliament, which sets policy for the EU, is far more strident on human rights issues than its member governments.
Officials and delegates at the meeting have said Portgual and the EU's insistence on a human rights clause is holding up a new treaty agreement outlining future ASEAN-EU ties.

ASEAN Secretary General Ajit Singh told the news conference many of the projects envisioned in such a new agreement are being adopted anyway, including some mentioned in this meeting's Final Declaration.
Both Jayakumar and Van Mierlo insisted that weaving closer economic ties between the blocs could survive the political differences.
"Would the fact we have different approaches make it impossible to have economic cooperation or other cooperation endeavours?" Jayakumar asked.

"I think a very heartening aspect of the Singaporean meeting is we were able to do both," he said. Although there were strong differences, "we did not let that overshadow the tone and spirit of the meeting."
